cards.title: Containers vs Virtual Machines (Namespaces & cgroups)
cards.question: Explain Containers vs Virtual Machines (Namespaces & cgroups)
cards.answer_30s: VMs virtualize hardware and run a full guest OS via a hypervisor, taking minutes to boot and gigabytes of RAM. Docker containers share the host Linux kernel, isolating what a process can see via namespaces (PID, NET, MNT, UTS, IPC, USER) and limiting what it can consume via cgroups (CPU, memory, I/O).
cards.typical_use: Packaging reproducible services across local dev, CI, and production clusters.
pitfalls: Clearly state: namespaces = isolation/visibility; cgroups = resource accounting and limits.

cards.title: Union Filesystem (OverlayFS) & Copy-on-Write
cards.question: Explain Union Filesystem (OverlayFS) & Copy-on-Write
cards.answer_30s: Docker images consist of immutable read-only layers stacked via OverlayFS (lowerdir). When a container starts, Docker adds one thin writable layer (upperdir) on top; modifying an existing file triggers Copy-on-Write (CoW) into the writable layer, while container restarts wipe ephemeral writes unless mounted to a volume.

code.body:
docker history my-image:latest
docker system df -v

cards.typical_use: Understanding why containers share base layers on disk and why writable layers shouldn't store persistent state.
pitfalls: Deleting a large file in a later RUN layer does not shrink image size because the file still exists in the lower read-only layer—chain commands in one RUN or use multi-stage builds.

cards.title: Multi-Stage Builds & Layer Caching
cards.question: Explain Multi-Stage Builds & Layer Caching
cards.answer_30s: Multi-stage builds compile dependencies in a builder image and copy only runtime artifacts into a slim/distroless final image, cutting image size by 80-90%. Ordering instructions from least-changed (dependencies) to most-changed (source code) maximizes build cache hits.

code.body:
FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --prefix=/install -r requirements.txt

FROM python:3.11-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /install /usr/local
COPY . .
USER 10001
CMD ["uvicorn", "main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0"]

cards.typical_use: Slashing CI/CD build times and container pull latency during autoscaling.
pitfalls: Always include a .dockerignore file (.git, node_modules, __pycache__, .env) to keep build context small and avoid leaking secrets.

cards.title: Non-Root Users, Capabilities & Image Scanning
cards.question: Explain Non-Root Users, Capabilities & Image Scanning
cards.answer_30s: Containers run as root (UID 0) by default, which increases blast radius on container escape. Production Dockerfiles must create and switch to a non-root USER, drop unnecessary Linux capabilities, use minimal/distroless bases, and run Trivy/Snyk CVE scans in CI.

code.body:
RUN addgroup --system app && adduser --system --group app
USER app
# Run with read-only rootfs:
# docker run --read-only --cap-drop=ALL --security-opt=no-new-privileges my-img

cards.typical_use: Hardening production workloads for SOC2/PCI compliance.
pitfalls: Never bake secrets via ENV or ARG in a Dockerfile—they remain visible in `docker history` and image manifests.

cards.title: Docker Networking Modes (Bridge, Host, None, Overlay)
cards.question: Explain Docker Networking Modes (Bridge, Host, None, Overlay)
cards.answer_30s: Default bridge networks isolate containers on a virtual subnet with NAT; user-defined bridges add automatic DNS resolution by container name. Host mode shares the host network stack (zero NAT overhead, no port isolation); overlay networks span multiple Docker Swarm/cluster hosts.

code.body:
docker network create --driver bridge app-net
docker run -d --network app-net --name db postgres:16
docker run -d --network app-net --name api my-api:latest

cards.typical_use: Connecting multi-container local stacks cleanly by service name.
pitfalls: The default `bridge` network does NOT support automatic DNS name resolution between containers—always create a user-defined bridge or use Docker Compose.

cards.title: Volumes vs Bind Mounts vs tmpfs
cards.question: Explain Volumes vs Bind Mounts vs tmpfs
cards.answer_30s: Named volumes are managed by Docker (/var/lib/docker/volumes), portable, and optimal for persistent DB data. Bind mounts map a specific host path (great for local hot-reload dev). tmpfs mounts store sensitive/ephemeral data strictly in host RAM.

code.body:
docker run -d -v pg_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:16
docker run -d --mount type=tmpfs,destination=/app/tmp my-app

cards.typical_use: Persisting database state across container recreations and keeping dev hot-reload fast.
pitfalls: On macOS/Windows, large bind mounts (like node_modules) can be slow across the VM boundary; use named volumes or cached mounts.

cards.title: PID 1, Signals (SIGTERM) & Graceful Shutdown
cards.question: Explain PID 1, Signals (SIGTERM) & Graceful Shutdown
cards.answer_30s: The container entrypoint runs as PID 1, which in Linux does not get default signal handlers for SIGTERM/SIGINT unless explicitly registered, and must reap zombie child processes. Using exec-form CMD/ENTRYPOINT or `--init` (tini) ensures SIGTERM reaches the app for graceful connection draining.
cards.typical_use: Eliminating 502 errors and dropped requests during rolling deployments.
pitfalls: Shell-form `CMD python main.py` wraps the process in `/bin/sh -c`, which may swallow SIGTERM and force a 10s wait before SIGKILL (exit 137).

cards.title: Healthchecks & Compose Dependency Ordering
cards.question: Explain Healthchecks & Compose Dependency Ordering
cards.answer_30s: Docker HEALTHCHECK periodically runs a command inside the container to mark it healthy or unhealthy. In Docker Compose, `depends_on` with `condition: service_healthy` ensures the API waits until PostgreSQL or Redis is actually accepting connections, not just started.

code.body:
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 5
  api:
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy

cards.typical_use: Preventing race-condition crashes on startup in multi-service stacks.
pitfalls: Healthcheck commands should verify process readiness cheaply without creating heavy DB load.

cards.title: Q: What is the difference between COPY and ADD, and CMD vs ENTRYPOINT?
cards.question: Q: What is the difference between COPY and ADD, and CMD vs ENTRYPOINT?
cards.answer_30s: A: COPY simply copies local files into the image; ADD also auto-extracts local tarballs and can fetch URLs (less predictable, so prefer COPY). ENTRYPOINT sets the fixed executable, while CMD provides default arguments that can be overridden via `docker run <image> <args>`.
cards.typical_use: Building flexible CLI and microservice images.
pitfalls: Recommend COPY over ADD in almost all cases for transparency and cache predictability.

cards.title: Q: What does Exit Code 137 or 139 mean when a container crashes?
cards.question: Q: What does Exit Code 137 or 139 mean when a container crashes?
cards.answer_30s: A: Exit code = 128 + signal number. 137 (128+9) means SIGKILL, almost always triggered by the Linux OOM Killer exceeding the container's cgroup memory limit (or `docker stop` timing out after 10s). 139 (128+11) means SIGSEGV (segmentation fault in native code). 143 (128+15) means clean SIGTERM.
cards.typical_use: Rapidly triaging crashing containers in production.
pitfalls: Always check `State.OOMKilled` first when seeing exit code 137.

cards.title: Q: Why did my Docker image end up 1.2GB even though I deleted temp files?
cards.question: Q: Why did my Docker image end up 1.2GB even though I deleted temp files?
cards.answer_30s: A: Each RUN instruction creates an immutable layer. Deleting files in a subsequent RUN only adds a whiteout marker in the new layer; the original bytes remain in the previous layer. Fix by chaining `apt-get install && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*` in a single RUN, using `--no-cache-dir`, and using multi-stage builds.

code.body:
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends gcc \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

cards.typical_use: Optimizing container image size and security footprint.
pitfalls: Also mention BuildKit cache mounts (`RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip`) to speed up builds without bloating layers.

cards.title: Q: How do you debug a container that crashes immediately or lacks shell tools?
cards.question: Q: How do you debug a container that crashes immediately or lacks shell tools?
cards.answer_30s: A: Check `docker logs --tail 200 <id>` and `docker inspect <id>`. Override the entrypoint with `docker run --rm -it --entrypoint /bin/sh <image>` to inspect the filesystem/env. For distroless images without a shell, use `docker debug` or `kubectl debug` ephemeral sidecar containers sharing the PID/network namespace.
cards.typical_use: Troubleshooting startup failures and distroless production containers.
pitfalls: Mention `docker exec -it` only works on running containers, whereas `--entrypoint` starts a fresh debug container.

cards.title: Q: How does Docker BuildKit improve builds and handle build-time secrets safely?
cards.question: Q: How does Docker BuildKit improve builds and handle build-time secrets safely?
cards.answer_30s: A: BuildKit builds independent stages in parallel, uses content-addressable caching, and supports `--mount=type=secret` so private SSH keys or npm/pip tokens are mounted temporarily during a RUN step and never persisted in any image layer.
cards.typical_use: Accessing private package registries securely in CI/CD pipelines.
pitfalls: This directly answers how to use private repos in Docker without leaking credentials in image history.

cards.title: Q: What is the difference between `docker run`, `docker compose`, and Kubernetes?
cards.question: Q: What is the difference between `docker run`, `docker compose`, and Kubernetes?
cards.answer_30s: A: `docker run` manages a single container on one host. `docker compose` declaratively orchestrates multi-container stacks on a single host (great for local dev and simple deployments). Kubernetes orchestrates containers across a cluster of nodes with automated scheduling, self-healing, rolling updates, service discovery, and horizontal autoscaling.
cards.typical_use: Explaining container orchestration boundaries in system design interviews.
pitfalls: Keep it pragmatic: don't over-engineer with Kubernetes if a single-host Compose or managed PaaS meets scale.
